extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of 18th‑century epistolary satire / general readers of satirical fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting and evaluating epistolary (letter‑based) satirical fiction that relies on voice, social observation, and anecdote to characterise and critique society. Emphasis on narrative manner, character detail, and ethical/financial realities of the literary world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner (style) as primary source of amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: “your amusement must arise, not from the matter, but from the manner, which you know is all my own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise distinctive narrative voice, wit, and stylistic manner over relying solely on incident or plot; a memoir/letter can be entertaining even when materially 'barren' if the manner is vivid. Example: the narrator claims readers enjoy his letters for manner rather than event. Anti‑pattern: flat, impersonal prose where style fails to compensate for thin action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage and the obligations of benefactors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those who are in distress he supplies with money when he has it, and with his credit when he is out of cash... When they want business, he either finds employment for them in his own service, or recommends them to booksellers...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting literary patronage, show reciprocal obligations and social entanglements: patrons supply money, credit, work, and table; beneficiaries may become dependent and impertinent. Use concrete episodes (bailouts, employment, lodging) to show the dynamics. Evaluate scenes by how plausibly they render economic and social dependency between patron and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical impartiality and the risks of censure
rubrics_metrics.description: “S-- directs a literary journal, in which their productions are necessarily brought to trial... the slightest censure... has rankled in the hearts of those authors to such a degree, that they have taken immediate vengeance on the critic in anonymous libels, letters, and lampoons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray literary criticism as a public trial: candid, impartial reviews may win enemies. As a writer of criticism or as a character who is a critic, be aware that even mild, fair censure can provoke vindictive responses. Use this dynamic as a plot/character device (backlash, anonymous attacks). Anti‑pattern: naive depiction that criticism has no social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship, attribution, and appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: “they do not even scruple to arrogate to themselves the merit of some of his performances, and have been known to sell their own lucubrations as the produce of his brain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat questions of credit and false attribution as a visible ethical faultline in literary circles. Scenes or evaluations should note plagiarism, false ascription, and the sale/passing‑off of works. Anti‑pattern: glossing over or sentimentalising appropriation; good depiction highlights stakes (reputation, survival).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic insecurity of the literary profession
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is at best but a desperate resource against starving, as it affords no provision for old age and infirmity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the precariousness of making a living by letters: old age, infirmity, humiliating dependence, irregular pay. When crafting characters who are writers, include realistic pressures (drudging for low pay, charity reliance) to ground satire and motive. Use as a criterion when evaluating plausibility of a writer's choices or compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using anecdote and social detail to satirise character
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator recounts concrete episodes (bailouts, disguises, alehouse incident, methodist meetings, presents, quarrels) to expose folly: e.g., guests who personated S-- and had their heads broken; the minister preaching in a lane; Lady Griskin’s officious meddling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire proceeds by vivid, specific anecdotes and social detail: small scenes (a fan flirt, an awkward present, a pulpit appearance) that reveal hypocrisy, vanity, and class foibles. Evaluate whether scenes are concrete and particular enough to sustain ironic distance; avoid abstract denunciation without illustrative episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary voice and variation by recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: The text is delivered as letters to varied recipients, altering tone: from confiding to playful to officious—e.g., letters to Miss Laetitia Willis, Sir Watkin Phillips, Dr Lewis, each with differing intimacy and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the epistolary form to modulate voice and perspective: tailor register, confession, and rhetorical aims to the intended correspondent. Letters should reveal character through how the narrator chooses what to disclose and how. Anti‑pattern: identical tone across all letters that flattens character; good practice exploits recipient variation for dramatic irony and depth.
